difficultyReason: Controlled-study stimulus whose conclusion rides on an unstated methodological assumption: that the enrollment criterion did not preselect for spontaneous recovery. Correct answer reveals hidden confounding in the sample. Trap (C) strengthens by ruling out an unrelated confound; trap (D) attacks the magnitude of the result without touching causation; trap (E) is out-of-scope comparative.
stimulus: Researcher: In a 12-month trial, patients with chronic lower-back pain who received biweekly acupuncture reported an average 42 percent reduction in pain, whereas a control group receiving sham needling reported only a 19 percent reduction. Because the two groups were otherwise similar in age, baseline pain, and prior treatment history, the results show that the therapeutic insertion of acupuncture needles is itself producing the additional pain reduction.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the researcher's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enrollment in the trial was restricted to patients whose pain had persisted for at least six months and had recently intensified — a pattern statistically associated with imminent natural remission independent of any treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The acupuncturists who administered the therapeutic needling had, on average, several more years of clinical experience than the practitioners who administered the sham procedure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither the patients nor the outcome assessors were informed of which group any given patient had been assigned to.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 42 percent reduction in self-reported pain is smaller than the reductions reported in trials of several newer pharmacological therapies for chronic lower-back pain.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sham needling has itself been shown in earlier studies to produce modest reductions in pain relative to no treatment at all.

explanations.correct: The researcher concludes that therapeutic needling itself is doing the extra work. (A) reveals a hidden selection effect: enrollment was keyed to patients poised for natural remission. If both arms improved from that baseline, the differential between arms still needs explaining — but (A) also implies that patients most prone to spontaneous improvement were precisely the kind the trial attracted, and any systematic imbalance in how fully that regression plays out across arms now confounds the comparison. More importantly, the conclusion requires that the 23-point gap reflect something therapeutic needles do; (A) undermines the assumption that the arms were comparably positioned with respect to natural recovery trajectories.
explanations.B: This is a live weakener candidate — experience gap is a real confound — but it is weaker than (A) because the conclusion is about whether the needles themselves did the work, and skilled handling of needles is still therapeutic needling. Reconsider against (A), which undermines the more basic assumption that the differential is not an artifact of the enrollment pool.
explanations.C: Strengthens — double-blinding protects against expectation effects.
explanations.D: Comparative magnitude vs. other treatments is out of scope; the argument is about whether needling caused the observed reduction, not whether it is the best therapy available.
explanations.E: If anything, this strengthens the study's design rationale (sham produced a real 19 percent reduction), and it does not undercut the inference that the additional reduction came from therapeutic needling.

difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in medicine: gut-bacteria composition → inflammatory markers → depressive symptoms. Correct answer exposes a mechanism operating in the opposite direction on the first link. Trap (B) strengthens by replicating; trap (D) is a subsidiary-point attack.
stimulus: Clinical researcher: Patients suffering major depressive disorder show, on average, markedly lower diversity of gut bacteria than matched healthy controls, and they also show elevated levels of circulating inflammatory cytokines. Since bacterial diversity is known to modulate cytokine production, and inflammation is increasingly implicated in depression, we conclude that the impoverished gut flora of depressed patients is a contributing cause of their depressive symptoms.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the researcher's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytokine levels in depressed patients vary substantially from week to week, depending on diet and sleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A separate study replicated the finding that bacterial diversity in depressed patients is lower than in matched controls.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The loss of appetite and disturbed eating patterns that characterize major depressive disorder have been shown, in animal models, to reliably produce substantial reductions in gut bacterial diversity within weeks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cytokine levels in some patients with major depressive disorder fall within the normal range.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Certain antidepressant medications have been observed to modestly increase gut bacterial diversity over the course of treatment.

explanations.correct: The researcher infers that poor gut flora helps cause depression. (C) reveals a mechanism running the opposite direction on the first link: depression itself, via its effect on eating, reliably degrades gut diversity. The observed correlation would then be an effect of depression rather than a cause of it, undermining the causal claim.
explanations.A: Week-to-week variability doesn't touch the averaged group comparison the argument relies on.
explanations.B: Strengthens — a replicated correlation supports the premise, not the conclusion's causal direction.
explanations.D: Attacks a subsidiary descriptive claim (that cytokines are elevated) without challenging the core causal inference; the average can still be elevated even if some individuals are normal.
explanations.E: Consistent with either causal direction. If antidepressants work and happen to raise diversity, this says nothing about whether diversity is upstream of depression.

difficultyReason: Comparative economic argument that treats two minimum-wage jurisdictions as matched. Correct answer reveals hidden confounding in the comparison baseline. Trap (A) is an opposite-answer strengthener; trap (D) is out-of-scope.
stimulus: Economist: Cities that raised their minimum wage above the state floor between 2018 and 2022 saw, on average, no larger increase in restaurant prices than demographically similar cities whose minimum wage remained at the state floor. Since restaurant pricing is especially sensitive to labor costs, this pattern shows that recent minimum-wage increases did not, on net, push consumer prices upward in the cities that adopted them.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the economist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Restaurants in the cities that raised their minimum wage reported, on average, the same profit margins in 2022 as they had reported in 2018.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Restaurants in many of the cities that retained the state floor operated under long-standing collective-bargaining agreements that committed them to wage increases matching or exceeding those mandated in the neighboring cities that raised their minimum wage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cities that adopted minimum-wage increases were slightly more populous, on average, than the comparison cities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nationally, restaurant prices rose more slowly between 2018 and 2022 than prices for grocery staples.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Several of the cities that raised their minimum wage also simplified their restaurant licensing procedures during the same period.

explanations.correct: The argument's comparison assumes the control cities had meaningfully lower labor-cost pressure. (B) dissolves that assumption: the 'no-increase' cities were already absorbing comparable wage increases through collective bargaining. With both groups facing similar labor-cost pressure, the absence of a price differential is uninformative about what minimum-wage policy itself would do.
explanations.A: Strengthens, if anything — stable margins alongside stable prices suggest the labor cost did not force a price increase, consistent with the economist's conclusion.
explanations.C: Population difference is described as slight and is not shown to bear on pricing dynamics.
explanations.D: National restaurant-versus-grocery comparisons don't speak to whether minimum-wage increases pushed restaurant prices up within the studied cities.
explanations.E: Licensing simplification, if anything, might lower costs and thereby reinforce the observed pattern — but it does not undermine the causal inference about minimum-wage policy; it introduces another downward pressure without isolating the wage effect.

difficultyReason: Environmental-science argument whose conclusion rests on an unstated methodological premise about sampling timing. Correct answer attacks a measurement assumption without denying any stated fact. Trap (C) attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; trap (E) is out-of-scope.
stimulus: Conservation scientist: Surveys conducted over the past decade in the three largest salt marshes along the Cape Alaine coast have recorded populations of the saltmarsh sparrow that are, on average, 28 percent smaller than populations recorded a decade earlier in the same marshes. Since the marshes are otherwise undisturbed and no new predators have been documented, the sparrow's decline must be due to rising sea levels, which shorten the dry window during which the sparrows can fledge their nests.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the scientist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Historically, saltmarsh sparrow populations have fluctuated more dramatically from year to year than the populations of most other marsh-nesting birds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The marshes in question were never protected as sparrow reserves, and casual recreational traffic has increased modestly over the past decade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recent study estimates that fledging success in coastal salt marshes has declined in step with the lengthening of high-tide periods along the eastern seaboard generally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The decade-earlier surveys were performed during the saltmarsh sparrow's peak breeding season, whereas the recent surveys were performed several weeks later, after most of the year's fledglings had dispersed to adjacent upland scrub.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conservation efforts in marshes farther south have, in some cases, stabilized local saltmarsh sparrow populations through active nest-site management.

explanations.correct: The conclusion treats the 28 percent gap as a real population decline and attributes it to sea-level rise. (D) exposes a methodological flaw: the later surveys missed dispersed fledglings that the earlier surveys would have counted, so the apparent decline may be partly or wholly an artifact of when the birds were counted. The causal claim is stranded until that confound is resolved.
explanations.A: Year-to-year fluctuation doesn't explain a sustained ten-year drop across three marshes.
explanations.B: Introduces a minor alternative cause, but the traffic is described as a modest increase — a plausible but weaker weakener than (D), which undercuts the very existence of the decline.
explanations.C: Strengthens, if anything — it supports the sea-level-rise mechanism the scientist proposes.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the argument concerns three Cape Alaine marshes, not remote management efforts.

difficultyReason: Controlled-study argument about a technology intervention whose conclusion depends on the outcome metric capturing what it purports to capture. Correct answer reveals the metric is gameable in a way that breaks the inference. Trap (A) strengthens; trap (B) is an unwarranted comparison.
stimulus: Technology columnist: In a controlled experiment, one group of programmers was provided with an AI coding assistant and a second, matched group was not. Over four weeks, developers using the assistant closed 35 percent more tickets from their team's issue tracker than developers in the control group. Since issue-tracker tickets are the standard unit of programmer output at this company, the experiment shows that the AI assistant makes programmers meaningfully more productive.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the columnist's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Programmers in both groups reported similar levels of job satisfaction at the end of the experiment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The AI assistant was developed by a company that sells programming tools to large software firms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A substantial portion of the additional tickets closed by the AI-assisted group were later reopened by quality-assurance reviewers, who identified regressions and incomplete fixes that the control group's tickets did not exhibit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Programmers in the AI-assisted group spent roughly the same number of hours at their workstations as programmers in the control group.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Before the experiment began, both groups had been closing tickets at statistically indistinguishable rates.

explanations.correct: The conclusion depends on tickets-closed being a faithful measure of productive output. (C) shows it is not: a substantial share of the extra tickets contained regressions that had to be redone, so the raw count overstates real productivity gains. The metric the argument rests on is contaminated by work the AI group is effectively offloading onto later reviewers.
explanations.A: Irrelevant — the conclusion is about productivity, not satisfaction.
explanations.B: Attacks the source rather than the evidence; the experiment's results do not become less informative because the tool has a commercial origin.
explanations.D: Strengthens, if anything — equal hours with higher ticket counts sharpens the apparent productivity gain.
explanations.E: Strengthens — a matched baseline makes the post-experiment differential easier to attribute to the intervention.

difficultyReason: Multi-step causal chain in linguistics: bilingual childhood → denser neural pathways → resistance to age-related cognitive decline. Correct answer attacks the unstated assumption linking the observed endpoint to the proposed mechanism, not to an unrelated factor. Trap (B) is too narrow; trap (E) strengthens.
stimulus: Linguist: Adults who were raised bilingually from infancy consistently perform better on tests of executive function in late middle age than adults who were raised monolingually. Early bilingual experience is known to produce denser neural connections in brain regions responsible for switching between cognitive tasks. Since those same regions underlie executive function, we may conclude that the executive-function advantage observed in later life is itself produced by the dense neural architecture laid down during bilingual childhood.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most undermines the linguist's conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Longitudinal neuroimaging shows that the denser neural architecture associated with early bilingualism has, in most individuals, fully atrophied to monolingual baselines by a person's mid-thirties, whereas the adults studied were in their late fifties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bilingual adults in the studies were, on average, no more likely than the monolingual adults to have pursued advanced degrees.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Some adults who acquired a second language only in adulthood also show elevated scores on tests of executive function in late middle age.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Executive function encompasses several distinct abilities, and bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some of these abilities more clearly than on others.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The density of neural connections in task-switching regions correlates, in brain-imaging studies, with stronger scores on executive-function tests at every age examined.

explanations.correct: The argument attributes a late-life advantage specifically to the dense architecture laid down in childhood. (A) severs that link: by the time the advantage is measured, the architecture in question has atrophied. Whatever explains the late-life difference, it cannot be the surviving presence of childhood-built density. The proposed mechanism collapses.
explanations.B: Rules out one alternative explanation (education), which if anything mildly strengthens the argument.
explanations.C: Too narrow — at most this suggests there is more than one route to the executive-function advantage, not that the childhood-bilingualism route is wrong.
explanations.D: Attacks the uniformity of the advantage across subskills without touching the causal mechanism; the conclusion survives so long as the pattern holds on average.
explanations.E: Strengthens — it reinforces the density-to-executive-function link the argument relies on.

difficultyReason: Policy argument from a quasi-comparison between pre- and post-intervention windows. Correct answer exposes hidden confounding from a concurrent change that the argument ignores. Trap (A) strengthens via regression-adjacent reasoning; trap (D) is an out-of-scope fact.
stimulus: Policy analyst: After the city of Brenshaw adopted a mandatory counseling program for first-time nonviolent offenders four years ago, the three-year reoffense rate for participants fell from 34 percent, as measured in the four years preceding the program, to 22 percent in the years since. Opponents of the program point to various social changes over the same period, but none of those changes has been shown to affect reoffense rates in comparable cities. The drop therefore shows that the counseling program is reducing reoffense among its participants.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the analyst's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three-year reoffense rate among first-time nonviolent offenders in cities that did not adopt mandatory counseling held roughly constant over the same period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Concurrent with the launch of the counseling program, Brenshaw's prosecutor's office adopted a policy of declining to charge a category of low-level offenses that had previously been prosecuted, so the post-program population of 'first-time nonviolent offenders' now excludes a group historically responsible for a disproportionate share of reoffenses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The counseling program is considerably more expensive per participant than most comparable rehabilitative interventions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: In neighboring cities without mandatory counseling, reoffense rates for first-time nonviolent offenders are somewhat higher than the 22 percent now observed in Brenshaw.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A minority of offenders assigned to the program fail to complete its required sessions.

explanations.correct: The argument treats the two populations — pre- and post-program 'first-time nonviolent offenders' — as comparable, and attributes the drop in reoffense to the counseling. (B) dissolves that comparability: the post-program population has been quietly redefined to exclude a subgroup with especially high reoffense rates. The apparent drop could be entirely a composition effect. The counseling program's contribution is no longer supported.
explanations.A: Strengthens — comparison cities' flat trend makes the Brenshaw drop look intervention-specific.
explanations.C: Cost is irrelevant to whether the program works.
explanations.D: Strengthens — Brenshaw's rate is lower than neighboring rates, consistent with the program helping.
explanations.E: Non-completion doesn't undermine the claim about participants; the analyst's conclusion concerns those who participate.

difficultyReason: Historiographic argument drawing a causal inference from archival evidence. Correct answer reveals a sampling bias in the surviving record that undercuts the inference. Trap (A) is out-of-scope; trap (D) strengthens a subsidiary detail.
stimulus: Historian: In the merchant archives of the Hanseatic port of Vissen, letters written in the decade after the city's adoption of double-entry bookkeeping in 1472 show merchants referring to profit margins with far greater numerical specificity than letters written in the decade preceding that adoption. Since specificity about margins was a prerequisite for the kind of strategic pricing that enriched late-medieval merchants, the spread of double-entry bookkeeping in Vissen itself enabled the commercial sophistication observed after 1472.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the historian's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double-entry bookkeeping had been in use in several Italian mercantile cities for nearly two centuries before Vissen adopted it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Vissen archives preserve the correspondence of roughly the same number of merchants from the decade before 1472 as from the decade after.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A fire in 1515 destroyed the bulk of Vissen's pre-1472 merchant correspondence, and the surviving pre-1472 letters were preserved by a single guild whose members were among the city's least numerate merchants and whose letters chiefly concerned personal matters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several of the most numerically specific post-1472 letters are from merchants whose families had long been prominent in Vissen's commercial life.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Double-entry bookkeeping, as practiced in Vissen, required a formal apprenticeship of at least three years.

explanations.correct: The argument infers from a contrast in the surviving archival record that Vissen's merchants became more numerically sophisticated after 1472, and attributes that shift to the new bookkeeping. (C) exposes a crippling sampling bias: the pre-1472 record is a narrow, unrepresentative residue dominated by the city's least numerate merchants. The 'before' sample cannot be compared to the 'after' sample, so the observed contrast does not establish any change in Vissen's commercial practice.
explanations.A: Out of scope — Italian precedent does not affect what Vissen's own merchants did or why.
explanations.B: Strengthens, if anything — comparable merchant counts in the two decades would support the comparison.
explanations.D: Tangential; family prominence says nothing about whether numeric specificity in the record reflects a real change.
explanations.E: Provides background on how the practice spread but does not undermine the inference from the letters.

difficultyReason: Legal-reform argument with a two-step predictive chain: proposed rule will change judicial behavior, which in turn will reduce appellate reversals. Correct answer attacks the hidden assumption linking the rule to judicial behavior. Trap (B) attacks a premise without touching the conclusion; trap (D) strengthens.
stimulus: Legal scholar: A proposed rule of appellate procedure would require trial judges to file, along with every contested ruling, a brief written statement summarizing the legal authorities on which the ruling rests. Judges who know that their reasoning will be laid out for inspection will take more care in forming that reasoning, and better-reasoned rulings are less likely to be overturned on appeal. If the proposed rule is adopted, therefore, the rate at which trial-court rulings are reversed on appeal will fall.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the legal scholar's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The appellate court that would review these cases already reverses trial-court rulings at a historically low rate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Some of the legal authorities trial judges would cite in their written statements are difficult to locate and annotate in the course of a working day.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The written statements would be made available to appellate courts, which would use them to identify, with a precision not currently available, errors of legal reasoning in rulings whose written record is today too sparse for such errors to be confidently detected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Trial judges who currently take especially detailed notes on their own reasoning are reversed on appeal at lower rates than judges who do not.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposed rule would apply only to contested rulings in civil cases, which make up the majority of the appellate court's docket.

explanations.correct: The conclusion predicts fewer reversals. The argument's two steps — better reasoning follows, reversals then fall — assume the appellate court's ability to detect reversible error remains constant. (C) undermines that hidden assumption: the same written statements that are supposed to improve reasoning also enable appellate courts to catch errors they would previously have missed. Reversals could therefore rise or remain flat even if the reasoning improves. The predictive chain is broken.
explanations.A: Irrelevant to whether the new rule will further reduce the rate; a low baseline can still fall.
explanations.B: Attacks the practicality of the rule, not the argument's conclusion about reversal rates.
explanations.D: Strengthens — it independently supports the link between detailed reasoning and fewer reversals.
explanations.E: Scope of application; does not undermine the mechanism.

difficultyReason: Arts argument with a multi-step causal chain: funding shift → composition time → ambition of works. Correct answer attacks the crucial middle link — that the funding shift actually increased usable composition time. Trap (C) strengthens; trap (E) is an unwarranted comparison.
stimulus: Music critic: When the Thaller Foundation restructured its grants to composers in 2015, it shifted from one-year fellowships to three-year fellowships of equivalent annual value. Longer fellowships insulate composers from commissioning pressures, and composers insulated from commissioning pressures produce more ambitious works. Indeed, works produced by Thaller fellows after 2015 have been reviewed as markedly more ambitious than works produced by Thaller fellows in the decade before. The restructuring, then, is what has enabled the ambition of the recent Thaller-funded output.
questionStem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the critic's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reviewers who assess the ambition of new compositions sometimes disagree substantially about a given work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thaller fellows typically accept the commissions offered to them, and beginning in 2014 the Thaller Foundation required its fellows to sign exclusive commissioning agreements with the foundation's own concert series — agreements that specify deadlines stricter than the deadlines associated with most outside commissions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Since 2015, Thaller fellows have reported higher satisfaction with their working conditions than fellows reported before the restructuring.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rival foundation, which did not restructure its grants, has over the same period also seen its fellows' work reviewed as more ambitious.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Some of the most ambitious works produced by Thaller fellows before 2015 remain more widely performed today than most works produced by Thaller fellows after 2015.

explanations.correct: The argument's causal chain requires that the longer fellowships actually reduce commissioning pressure on composers. (B) negates exactly that middle link: in conjunction with the restructuring, the foundation bound fellows to commissioning agreements with stricter deadlines than the outside commissions they would otherwise have faced. The increase in nominal fellowship length did not translate into insulation from commissioning pressure. The proposed mechanism for the observed ambition is cut.
explanations.A: Minor reviewer disagreement is consistent with a real average shift; it does not disturb the conclusion.
explanations.C: Strengthens, if anything — better working conditions align with the argument's picture of relieved composers.
explanations.D: Weakens somewhat by suggesting a period-wide rise in ambition that has nothing to do with Thaller's restructuring, but it does not foreclose that Thaller's own policy contributed. (B) more directly severs the argument's internal mechanism and is the stronger answer.
explanations.E: Unwarranted comparison — the durability of older works doesn't speak to whether the restructuring boosted recent ambition.
